example_english: In winter, it snows a lot, so I stay warm at home and relax.
usage_note: Season noun; can combine with words like ‘봄/여름/가을’ or modifiers (겨울철, 한겨울).

example_english: In autumn the weather is cool, so it's nice to go for walks.
usage_note: Refers to the season 'autumn' (fall); commonly used in everyday contexts.

example_korean: 한국에는 사계절이 뚜렷해서 계절마다 풍경이 달라요.
example_english: In Korea there are four distinct seasons, so the scenery changes with each season.
usage_note: '계절' means 'season' as in time of year; often used with numbers or descriptors (봄, 여름, 가을, 겨울).

example_english: I got a zero on the exam today.
usage_note: 공 means the numeral zero; homonymous with other words (e.g., ball: 공).

example_english: The first gift is very special.
usage_note: 첫번째 is a written form; 첫 번째 (with a space) is common for ordinal counting in Korean.

example_english: My second daughter entered university this year.
usage_note: 둘째 can mean 'second child' or 'second in order'; context clarifies which is intended.

example_english: He arrived third and took a seat.
usage_note: 세번째 indicates ordinal 'third' and follows native Korean numbering patterns (첫·두번째, 세번째).

example_english: He was the fourth to present in the class.
usage_note: 네번째 is an ordinal noun meaning 'fourth'; can be used with counters or positions.

example_english: He gave the fifth presentation.
usage_note: Ordinal '다섯번째' indicates position in order; often interchangeable with '다섯 번째' (two-word form).

example_english: Shall I tell you my phone number?
usage_note: 번호 commonly means a numeric identifier (phone, room, ticket); not a counting counter.

example_english: In January we have a New Year's party with family.
usage_note: 일월 is a formal or literary way to say January; 일월 is less common in casual speech than 1월.

example_english: The full moon looks brightest in February.
usage_note: 이월 is a formal/old-fashioned term for February; commonly used in formal writing or lunar-calendar contexts.

example_english: A lot of flowers bloom in March.
usage_note: Refers to the month March (third month); used in calendars and dates.

example_korean: 저는 사월에 한국으로 여행을 갈 거예요.
example_english: I will travel to Korea in April.
usage_note: 사월 is the Sino-Korean word for the month April (formal written style, used in dates).

example_english: Many flowers bloom in May.
usage_note: 오월 means the month of May (literary/slightly formal tone); common everyday word is 5월.

example_english: Our wedding will be in June.
usage_note: 유월 means the month of June; formal word but common in dates and announcements.

example_korean: 우리 가족은 칠월에 바다로 여행을 가요.
example_english: My family goes on a trip to the beach in July.
usage_note: 칠월 is the month name 'July' in Korean; used like other month names (e.g., 일월, 이월).

example_english: I am going to travel to Korea in August.
usage_note: 팔월 is the native Korean name for the month August; used in dates and casual speech.

example_english: My birthday is in September.
usage_note: 구월 is a formal/literary word for 'September' (commonly '9월' in everyday use).

example_english: In October, the autumn leaves color beautifully.
usage_note: 시월 is a traditional/literary term for October; equivalent to 10월 in modern usage.

example_english: In November the weather gradually gets colder.
usage_note: 십일월 is the Sino-Korean term for the month November (11th month).

example_korean: 우리 가족은 십이월에 크리스마스 파티를 해요.
example_english: My family has a Christmas party in December.
usage_note: 십이월 is the Sino-Korean name for the month December (formal calendar use).

example_english: We will have a meeting next Monday.
usage_note: 월요일 is a weekday noun meaning Monday; can be combined with 요일 markers (e.g., 다음, 지난).

example_english: I have a meeting next Tuesday.
usage_note: Common weekday noun; used with 시간 expressions (e.g., 다음, 이번, 지난).

example_english: Shall we go to see a movie with a friend on Wednesday?
usage_note: Refers to the weekday Wednesday; used like other day-of-week nouns in Korean.

example_english: The meeting is held on Thursday afternoon.
usage_note: Standard noun for the weekday 'Thursday'; not formal. Use with 날짜/time expressions.

example_english: I'm going to have dinner with a friend on Friday.
usage_note: 금요일 simply denotes the weekday Friday; used in calendar/time expressions.

example_korean: 이번 주 토요일에 친구들과 영화를 볼 거예요.
example_english: I'm going to watch a movie with friends this Saturday.
usage_note: 토요일 simply means Saturday; common in calendars and scheduling contexts.

example_english: I watch a movie with friends on Sunday.
usage_note: 일요일 is a weekday name meaning 'Sunday'; used for days of the week in calendars and schedules.

example_english: This year I have turned twenty-five years old.
usage_note: 년 is a counter/suffix for years; attach to numerals (e.g., 2021년, 3년).

example_korean: 회의가 한 시간쯤 걸릴 것 같아요.
example_english: The meeting will probably take about one hour.
usage_note: 시간 can mean a duration or the concept of time; use '한 시간' for one-hour duration.

example_english: The meeting starts in 10 minutes.
usage_note: Homonym: 분 also means a polite counter for people; context determines meaning.

example_english: Do you want to go see the stars tonight?
usage_note: 밤 means 'night' as time period (evening to early morning); often used with 오늘/어젯밤/밤새.

example_english: I work as a nurse at a hospital.
usage_note: Common everyday verb meaning 'to work'; can take particles for location/role (e.g., ~에서, ~로).

example_english: I play/hang out with friends together at the park on the weekend.
usage_note: 놀다 can mean play or hang out; context decides whether it’s recreation or socializing.

example_korean: 저는 공원에서 매일 한 시간씩 걷습니다.
example_english: I walk in the park for an hour every day.
usage_note: 걷다 is the neutral verb 'to walk'; use 걷습니다/걸어요 depending on formality.

example_english: I run in the park every morning.
usage_note: Common verb for physical running; can also mean 'to operate' in technical contexts (not covered here).

example_korean: 오늘 아버지께서 저를 태우고 시내까지 운전해 주셨어요.
example_english: My father gave me a ride and drove me to downtown today.
usage_note: 운전하다 means to operate/drive a vehicle; use with subject who controls the vehicle.

example_english: The birds fly in the sky welcoming spring.
usage_note: 날다 primarily means to move through the air; can be literal or figurative (e.g., time/rumors "날다").

example_english: In summer, I swim in the sea with my friends.
usage_note: 수영하다 means to swim (verb); commonly used for recreational or athletic swimming.

example_english: I am going to Seoul tomorrow.
usage_note: 가다 is the basic verb 'to go'; use different endings for tense/formality (가요, 갔어요, 갈게요).

example_english: The bus suddenly stopped.
usage_note: 멈추다 is a generalverb meaning to stop or cease motion or action.

example_english: Walk following the route shown on the map.
usage_note: 따르다 can mean to physically follow or to obey/adhere to rules; context determines nuance.

example_korean: 저는 그 문제를 어떻게 해결할지 오랫동안 생각했어요.
example_english: I thought for a long time about how to solve that problem.
usage_note: 생각하다 can mean to consider or believe; context determines nuance.

example_korean: 그가 무슨 말을 하는지 잘 못 들었어요, 다시 말해 주세요.
example_english: I couldn't hear what he was saying clearly; please say it again.
usage_note: Common everyday verb for 'to speak' or 'to say'; can take direct objects (말을 하다).

example_english: Would you like to eat dinner together?
usage_note: Common everyday verb meaning 'to eat'; can also mean 'consume' or 'take' in other contexts.

example_english: Would you like to drink some water?
usage_note: Polite everyday form; 마시다 also means 'take' (medicine) in context.

example_korean: 그 범죄자는 결국 체포되어 법정에서 사형을 선고받아 처형되었지만, 우리는 누구도 죽이는 것을 정당화할 수 없습니다.
example_english: The criminal was eventually arrested, sentenced to death in court, and executed, but we cannot justify killing anyone.
usage_note: Formal and strong verb; can be literal or figurative (e.g., '죽이다' for killing or '웃겨서 죽겠다' colloquially).

example_korean: 그는 병으로 어제 세상을 떠나서 모두가 많이 슬펐어요.
example_english: He passed away from illness yesterday, and everyone was very sad.
usage_note: 죽다 is direct for 'to die'; use softer expressions (세상을 떠나다) in polite contexts.

example_korean: 그 농담을 듣고 모두가 함께 웃었어요.
example_english: Everyone laughed together when they heard that joke.
usage_note: 웃다 can mean both 'laugh' and 'smile' depending on context; here it denotes audible laughter.

example_korean: 아이가 밤새 울어서 잠을 제대로 못 잤어요.
example_english: The child cried all night, so I couldn't sleep properly.
usage_note: Standard verb for producing tears or crying; used for people and animals.

example_english: I bought fruit at the supermarket.
usage_note: 사다 means 'to buy'; common in everyday speech (past 샀어요), not formal honorific.

example_english: I paid the receipt amount by card.
usage_note: Formal verb for paying money; commonly for bills, fees, and official payments.

example_english: I sell used books online every weekend.
usage_note: 팔다 = to sell; pairs with items sold (e.g., 물건을 팔다).

example_english: He shot the gun at the target.
usage_note: 쏘다 can mean 'to shoot' (weapon/projectile) and also 'to sting' or 'to send' in other contexts; here it refers to firing a gun.

example_english: I am learning Korean.
usage_note: General verb for acquiring knowledge or skills; often used with -를 배우다 or 배우다 + -고 있다 for ongoing learning.

example_english: The children jump high on the playground.
usage_note: Common verb for physically jumping; can also be used figuratively (e.g., jump a task).

example_english: I smelled the puppy's leash.
usage_note: Used for actively sniffing or perceiving an odor; transitive verb taking the thing smelled as object.

example_english: If you listen to music well, your mood gets better.
usage_note: 듣다 can mean both 'to listen' (actively) and 'to hear' (passively); context clarifies intent.

example_korean: 수프를 먼저 한 입 맛봐도 될까요?
example_english: May I taste the soup first?
usage_note: 맛보다 = to taste/try food; polite request uses 맛보다 → 맛보다/맛봐요.

example_english: I go to the theater to see a movie.
usage_note: 보다 also means 'to look' or 'to try' in other contexts; here it specifically means 'to see/watch'.

example_korean: 그는 작품을 만지지 말라고 안내문을 읽었어요.
example_english: He read the notice that said not to touch the artwork.
usage_note: 만지다 = to touch; polite prohibition often uses ~지 말다. Avoid implying prolonged handling.

example_korean: 아기가 엄마에게 뽀뽀를 하려고 손을 내밀었어요.
example_english: The baby reached out to give his mother a kiss.
usage_note: Informal, affectionate action; commonly used for light/kissing gestures, not formal contexts.

example_english: A small trash can at home is burning.
usage_note: 불타다 is intransitive; use to describe something burning (not to burn something).

example_english: The snow melts in the warm sunlight.
usage_note: 녹다 is intransitive 'to melt' (not 'to melt something'); use 녹이다 for transitive form.

example_english: I am digging up potatoes in the garden.
usage_note: 파다 commonly means to dig physically; also used figuratively (e.g., '파고들다')—context defines literal vs. figurative use.

example_english: An old machine exploded at the factory.
usage_note: 폭발하다 is used for literal explosions and can describe emotional outbursts metaphorically.

example_english: Please sit on the chair.
usage_note: 앉다 is a general verb 'to sit'; use 앉아 주세요 for polite requests.

example_korean: 버스 멈추자마자 모두 일어서서 줄을 섰어요.
example_english: As soon as the bus stopped, everyone stood up and lined up.
usage_note: 서다 also means 'to be scheduled' or 'to stop'; here it means 'to stand' in a physical sense.

example_english: I really love that person.
usage_note: Used broadly for romantic or deep affection; can be both romantic and non-romantic depending on context.

example_english: A passerby opened the door for me.
usage_note: Common verb for people or things passing by; can mean 'to go past' or 'to pass (time)'.

example_english: I'm going to the hair salon to get my hair cut.
usage_note: 자르다 is a general verb for cutting physical things (hair, paper, trees); context shows what is cut.

example_korean: 형제들이 어제 밤에 작은 일로 싸웠어요.
example_english: The brothers fought last night over a small matter.
usage_note: Used for physical or verbal fights; neutral register, common in everyday speech.

example_english: I'm tired, so I'll lie down on the sofa.
usage_note: Standard verb meaning 'to lie down'; 주로 사람이나 동물이 몸을 눕히는 상황에서 사용.

example_english: We danced all night at the party.
usage_note: 춤추다 is a regular verb meaning 'to dance'; use past/present tense normally for actions.

example_korean: 어제 밤에 일찍 자서 오늘 기분이 좋아요.
example_english: I went to bed early last night, so I feel good today.
usage_note: Common verb meaning 'to sleep'; can also mean 'to lie down' in some contexts.

example_korean: 아침에 너무 일찍 깨서 다시 잠들기 어려워요.
example_english: I woke up too early in the morning, so it's hard to fall asleep again.
usage_note: 깨다 can mean to wake up or to break; here it means 'wake up'.

example_english: I sing with my friends every weekend.
usage_note: 노래하다 means 'to sing' (action); it’s commonly used for casual and formal contexts with appropriate politeness.

example_english: Shall we count the number of people?
usage_note: Used for counting items or people; homonym with 'strong' (세다) but here means 'to count'.

example_english: I am getting married next month.
usage_note: 결혼하다 means to marry or get married; use with 상대/사람 (e.g., ~와/과 결혼하다) to specify partner.

example_korean: 어려운 일이 있을 때마다 저는 조용히 기도해요.
example_english: Whenever I have a difficult time, I quietly pray.
usage_note: Used for religious or solemn expressions of prayer; polite verb form is 기도해요.

example_korean: 우리 팀이 경기에서 이겨서 더 기뻐요.
example_english: Our team won the match, so I'm happier.
usage_note: 이기다 means 'to win' (opponent or competition); used for games, debates, arguments.

example_korean: 우리 팀이 지난 경기에서 져서 많이 아쉬워요.
example_english: Our team lost the last match, so we're very disappointed.
usage_note: 지다 commonly means 'to lose' in contests; also used in meteorological phrases (e.g., 해가 지다) with different meanings.

example_english: Mix the sugar well into the bread dough.
usage_note: Common transitive verb for combining substances; also used figuratively for blending ideas or groups.

example_korean: 허리를 구부리면 등이 아플 수 있어요.
example_english: If you bend your waist, your back can hurt.
usage_note: 구부리다 means to bend something or oneself; common transitive use (object often omitted for body parts).

example_english: Wash your hands and eat.
usage_note: Common everyday verb for cleaning body, hands, or dishes; not for washing clothes (use 빨다).

example_korean: 오늘 저녁에 가족을 위해 한식을 요리해요.
example_english: I cook Korean food for my family tonight.
usage_note: 요리하다 generally means to prepare/cook food; can imply skillful preparation.

example_english: May I open the window?
usage_note: 열다 is a general verb for opening doors, windows, books, apps, etc.; use context to specify object.

example_english: Please close the window.
usage_note: Basic verb for closing physical or abstract things; polite request uses -아/어 주세요.

example_english: I write in my diary today.
usage_note: 쓰다 also means 'to use' or 'to wear' in other contexts; here it means 'to write'.

example_english: I will call (invite) my friend to my house.
usage_note: 부르다 can mean 'call' or 'invite'; context determines whether it's calling a name, phone, or inviting someone.

example_english: Try turning your head while looking in the mirror.
usage_note: 돌다 can mean physical turning or rotating; context determines whether subject moves or object rotates.

example_korean: 회사는 새로운 공장을 이번 해에 건설합니다.
example_english: The company will construct a new factory this year.
usage_note: 건설하다 is a formal verb for building/constructing structures (often used in news, business, and official contexts).

example_korean: 선생님이 새로운 문법을 학생들에게 친절하게 가르쳐요.
example_english: The teacher kindly teaches the new grammar to the students.
usage_note: 가르치다 is a general verb meaning 'to teach' or 'to instruct' used with people as recipients.

example_english: Children grow up quickly.
usage_note: Used for children, plants, or animals growing; also means 'to increase' in size or quantity in some contexts.

example_english: The children drew pictures on the wall, so it became brighter.
usage_note: 그리다 primarily means 'to draw' or 'paint'; context may require specific verb (쓰다 for write).

example_korean: 아기가 우유를 잘 먹어서 엄마가 직접 먹여요.
example_english: The baby is drinking milk well, so the mother feeds him/her directly.
usage_note: 먹이다 means to give food to someone/animal (causative of 먹다); used when one person feeds another.

example_english: The cat caught a fish.
usage_note: '잡다' is general 'to catch' or 'to grab'; context determines physical catching vs. seizing.

example_english: He threw the ball far.
usage_note: 던지다 is a general verb for physically throwing something; can be used figuratively (e.g., questions, blame).

example_english: I clean the house every Saturday.
usage_note: Common verb meaning 'to clean'; used for rooms, houses, offices, etc.

example_english: I can't find my keys.
usage_note: Common verb for both 'find' and 'look for'; requires object marked by 을/를 or contextual subject.

example_english: I was riding a bicycle on the road and fell down.
usage_note: Used for people or objects losing balance and falling; not for falling asleep or dropping intentionally.

example_english: Please push the door gently.
usage_note: Common everyday verb; can mean shove or postpone in different contexts (confirm context if needed).

example_korean: 문이 잘 안 열려서 손잡이를 당겼어요.
example_english: The door wasn't opening well, so I pulled the handle.
usage_note: 당기다 is a verb meaning 'to pull'; the part of speech given as noun is likely incorrect.

example_english: This bag is heavy, so it's hard to carry.
usage_note: 들다 here means 'to carry' (physical lifting); '들다' also has other senses like 'to cost'—context clarifies meaning.

example_korean: 어제 비 때문에 자전거가 망가져서 오늘 못 타요.
example_english: My bicycle broke down because of the rain yesterday, so I can't ride it today.
usage_note: 망가지다 describes something becoming broken or damaged (intransitive); use 망가뜨리다 for 'to break' (transitive).

example_english: The window broke because of the wind.
usage_note: 깨지다 is intransitive: something becomes broken (not someone breaking it).

example_english: I wore a new coat today.
usage_note: 입다 = to put on/wear clothing or accessories; contrasts with 벗다 (to take off).

example_korean: 그는 손으로 나무를 흔들어서 잎을 떨어뜨렸어요.
example_english: He shook the tree with his hand to make the leaves fall.
usage_note: 흔들다 is a general verb for shaking or waving; context determines whether it's physical or figurative.

example_english: Please sign the contract.
usage_note: Formal/action of writing one's signature; used for documents and agreements.

example_korean: 그는 화가 나서 나무로 그 상자를 세게 팼어요.
example_english: He got angry and beat/bashed the box hard with a piece of wood.
usage_note: Informal verb often describes physical hitting; can be violent—use contextually.

example_korean: 무거운 상자를 두 사람이 함께 들어올려서 창고에 넣었어요.
example_english: Two people lifted the heavy box together and put it in the storage room.
usage_note: 들어올리다 = to lift something upward (transitive); often physical lifting.

example_korean: 이 도로는 길어서 운전하는 데 시간이 오래 걸려요.
example_english: This road is long, so it takes a long time to drive.
usage_note: 길다 describes physical or temporal length/duration; can also be used figuratively.

example_korean: 이 치마는 제 키에 비해 너무 짧아요.
example_english: This skirt is too short for my height.
usage_note: 짧다 describes physical or temporal shortness; commonly adjective (descriptive verb) in Korean.

example_korean: 우리 아들은 키가 커서 농구를 좋아해요.
example_english: My son is tall, so he likes basketball.
usage_note: 키가 크다 describes someone's height; commonly used for people and animals.

example_korean: 제 동생은 키가 작아서 어린이용 옷이 잘 맞아요.
example_english: My younger sibling is short, so children's clothes fit well.
usage_note: 키가 작다 describes a person's height; commonly used informally about people or animals.

example_korean: 이 도로는 차가 지나가기에는 너무 넓어요.
example_english: This road is too wide for cars to pass through.
usage_note: 넓다 describes physical width or spaciousness; often used for places or objects.

example_korean: 이 방은 창문이 많아서 아주 커요.
example_english: This room has many windows, so it's very big.
usage_note: 크다 describes physical or abstract size; use 커요 for polite present affirmative form.

example_korean: 이 방은 창문이 작아서 햇빛이 잘 들어오지 않아요.
example_english: This room's window is small, so sunlight doesn't come in well.
usage_note: Used to describe physical or figurative smallness; common adjective-like verb (size).

example_korean: 컴퓨터가 너무 느려서 파일을 열 때 시간이 많이 걸려요.
example_english: The computer is so slow that it takes a long time to open files.
usage_note: 느리다 describes speed or pace; can refer to people, machines, or processes.

example_korean: 이 차는 속도가 빨라서 고속도로에서 편해요.
example_english: This car is fast, so it's comfortable on the highway.
usage_note: 빠르다 describes high speed or quickness; often used for people, vehicles, or processes.

example_korean: 수프가 너무 뜨거워서 바로 먹을 수 없어요.
example_english: The soup is too hot, so I can't eat it right away.
usage_note: Used for describing high temperature (objects, liquids); not for spicy heat.

example_english: My hands feel cold.
usage_note: 차겁다 describes physical coldness of objects or body parts; similar to 춥다 but used for touch/feeling.

example_korean: 오늘 날씨가 따뜻해서 공원에 가고 싶어요.
example_english: It's warm today, so I want to go to the park.
usage_note: 따뜻하다 describes ambient temperature or feelings of warmth; commonly used for weather, objects, and emotions.

example_korean: 가을 아침은 공기가 선선해서 산책하기 좋아요.
example_english: The autumn morning's air is cool, so it's good for a walk.
usage_note: Describes pleasantly cool weather or atmosphere; not very cold.

example_korean: 이 가게에는 항상 새롭고 흥미로운 물건들이 많아요.
example_english: This shop always has many new and interesting items.
usage_note: 새롭다 describes something being new or unfamiliar; often contrasts with 익숙하다 (familiar).

example_english: This book is old, so the cover is worn.
usage_note: Used for inanimate objects; describes age or worn condition.

example_korean: 그 배우는 실제로도 젊지만, 연기력도 좋아요.
example_english: That actor is actually young, and his acting skills are also good.
usage_note: 젊다 describes age or appearance—used for people, not things; common in casual/polite speech.

example_korean: 할아버지는 요즘 건강 때문에 많이 늙으셨어요.
example_english: My grandfather has aged a lot recently because of his health.
usage_note: 늙다 describes aging (people/animals); can be sensitive—use politely or with respectful forms.

example_english: The food at this restaurant is really good.
usage_note: Common adjective-like verb used to express approval or preference; can follow nouns or verbs (좋아하다).

example_korean: 이 음식은 조금 짜서 제 입맛에는 나쁘네요.
example_english: This food is a bit salty, so it's bad for my taste.
usage_note: 나쁘다 describes something unfavorable or not good; tone/context varies by degree.

example_english: It rained, so my clothes got wet.
usage_note: 젖다 describes becoming wet/damp; often used for clothes, hair, or surfaces.

example_korean: 오늘 날씨가 건조해서 목이 자주 아파요.
example_english: The weather is dry today, so my throat often hurts.
usage_note: Used for dry conditions (weather, skin); also describes fabric or materials; not a transitive 'to dry'.

example_english: My head kept hurting, so I went to bed early.
usage_note: 아프다 covers both feeling ill and physical pain; use subject markers to specify which body part feels pain.

example_english: These days I exercise every day, so my body is healthy.
usage_note: Used to describe physical or mental well-being; often with 있다/되다 or adjectives like 건강하다.

example_english: The library is so noisy that it's hard to study.
usage_note: 시끄럽다 describes noisy/loud environments or sounds; can describe people, places, or objects creating noise.

example_english: The library is quiet right now.
usage_note: Used to describe a quiet state (not noisy); commonly describes places or people.

example_korean: 오늘 가족과 함께 있어서 정말 행복해요.
example_english: I am really happy today because I am with my family.
usage_note: Used to describe feeling happy (state); commonly conjugated like an adjective in Korean (행복하다 → 행복해요).

example_korean: 그 소식을 듣고 저는 정말 슬펐어요.
example_english: I was really sad when I heard that news.
usage_note: Describes feeling sad; common adjective-like verb used with past/present forms (슬펐어요, 슬퍼요).

example_english: That flower is really beautiful.
usage_note: Descriptive adjective (verb in Korean grammar); often used for people, nature, art; polite contexts use -어요/습니다 forms.

example_korean: 그 배우는 사진보다 실제로 더 못생겨 보여요.
example_english: That actor looks uglier in person than in photos.
usage_note: Informal/neutral; can be rude—use carefully in conversation.

example_korean: 그 가게 주인은 귀머거리 손님에게 천천히 글로 설명해 드렸어요.
example_english: The shop owner slowly explained it in writing to the deaf customer.
usage_note: 귀머거리 is an older term; use 장애인 or 청각장애인 in formal/neutral contexts.

example_korean: 그는 어릴 때부터 시력을 잃어서 지금은 맹인으로 생활해요.
example_english: He lost his sight when he was young, so now he lives as a blind person.
usage_note: Formal term; often used in medical/legal contexts; '시각장애인' is a common alternative.

example_korean: 그 사람은 항상 착해서 친구들이 많아요.
example_english: That person is always kind, so they have many friends.
usage_note: Used to describe a person's kind or good-natured character in everyday situations.

example_korean: 그 가족은 오랫동안 가난해서 작은 집에서 살았어요.
example_english: That family was poor for a long time and lived in a small house.
usage_note: 가난하다 describes being poor (socioeconomic); can be sensitive—use respectfully.

example_korean: 그 가족은 대대로 부유해서 자식들에게 좋은 교육을 시켰어요.
example_english: That family has been wealthy for generations, so they provided good education for their children.
usage_note: 부유하다 is a formal verb meaning to be wealthy; used in written or polite contexts.

example_korean: 이 책은 종이가 너무 두껍아서 접기 힘들어요.
example_english: This book's paper is too thick, so it's hard to fold.
usage_note: 두껍다 describes physical thickness; can also be used metaphorically (e.g., skin, layers).

example_korean: 이 책은 종이가 얇아서 쉽게 찢어져요.
example_english: This book's paper is thin, so it tears easily.
usage_note: 얇다 describes physical thinness (layers or thickness), not thinness of people.

example_english: The prices at this shop are a bit expensive.
usage_note: Describes cost; commonly used to say something costs a lot (can modify with degree adverbs).

example_english: The fruit at this shop is cheap and fresh.
usage_note: 싸다 primarily means 'to be cheap'; can also mean 'to wrap' (different verb).

example_korean: 이 길은 공사 후에 아주 평탄해졌어요.
example_english: This road became very smooth/flat after the construction.
usage_note: Formal adjective often used for surfaces or terrain; not for emotional 'smoothness'.

example_korean: 이 철봉은 오래되어서 가운데가 구부러져 있어요.
example_english: This bar is old, so the middle is bent.
usage_note: Describes something becoming bent or curved (intransitive); often physical objects.

example_korean: 반지를 오른손 네 번째 손가락에 끼었어요.
example_english: I put a ring on (wore a ring on) the fourth finger of my right hand.
usage_note: 끼다 also means 'to get stuck' or 'to wear' for accessories like rings, gloves, glasses.
meaning: To put on or wear, to wear (a ring)

example_korean: 이 바지는 허리가 너무 헐렁해서 떨어질 것 같아요.
example_english: These pants are so loose at the waist that they feel like they will fall down.
usage_note: Describes clothing or fitting being loose; can also describe loose-fitting objects or arrangements.

example_korean: 이 건물은 주변 건물보다 훨씬 높아요.
example_english: This building is much taller than the surrounding buildings.
usage_note: Used to describe physical height or levels; can also mean high in degree (e.g., price, probability).

example_korean: 이 방은 천장이 낮아서 키 큰 사람이 불편할 수 있어요.
example_english: This room has a low ceiling, so tall people might be uncomfortable.
usage_note: Used to describe physical height or level; often contrasts with '높다' (high).

example_english: This bread is old, so it's hard.
usage_note: Used for textures or manners (can mean rigid or formal); here denotes physical hardness.

example_korean: 이 베개는 정말 부드러워서 잠이 잘 와요.
example_english: This pillow is really soft, so I fall asleep easily.
usage_note: Describes texture or touch; can also describe taste, voice, or manner (soft).

example_english: The lake water is deeper than I thought.
usage_note: Used for physical depth or abstract depth (e.g., feelings); polite everyday form.

example_korean: 이 호수는 물이 얕아서 아이들이 안전하게 놀 수 있어요.
example_english: The water in this lake is shallow, so children can play safely.
usage_note: Used for physical depth; can describe water, containers, or figurative 'superficiality'.

example_korean: 이 방은 창문을 열어서 공기를 바꾸면 더 깨끗해져요.
example_english: This room becomes cleaner if you open the windows to refresh the air.
usage_note: Describes a state of being clean; often used for places, objects, or appearance.

example_korean: 바닥이 아주 더러워서 신발을 벗고 들어가세요.
example_english: The floor is very dirty, so please take off your shoes before entering.
usage_note: Common everyday adjective meaning 'dirty'; often describes places, clothes, or objects.

example_korean: 그 남자 친구는 힘이 세서 무거운 가구도 혼자 옮겨요.
example_english: That boyfriend is strong, so he moves heavy furniture by himself.
usage_note: Used to describe physical strength; often about people or animals.

example_korean: 그 약은 제 증상에 비해 효과가 약해요.
example_english: That medicine is weak for my symptoms.
usage_note: 약하다 can describe physical strength, flavors, effects, or intensity (weaker/not strong).

example_english: I have been living in Seoul for ten years.
usage_note: General verb for residing; also used figuratively (e.g., '살다' = 'to experience' in some contexts).

example_korean: 이상한 냄새가 나서 가방이 무거운 것 같아요.
example_english: My bag seems heavy because there is a strange smell.
usage_note: 무겁다 describes physical weight or figurative heaviness; context determines literal vs. metaphorical use.

example_korean: 이 가방은 내용물이 거의 없어서 아주 가벼워요.
example_english: This bag is very light because it hardly has any contents.
usage_note: 가볍다 describes physical weight or light feeling; also used metaphorically (e.g., mood).

example_english: The room is dark because it's night.
usage_note: 어둡다 describes low light or mood; commonly used for places or atmospheres.

example_korean: 이 방은 창문이 커서 항상 밝아요.
example_english: This room is always bright because the windows are large.
usage_note: Used for light/brightness or cheerful atmosphere; context determines literal vs. figurative meaning.

example_korean: 그 가수는 젊은이들 사이에서 인기가 많아요.
example_english: That singer is very popular among young people.
usage_note: Describes general popularity; used for people, items, or ideas.

example_english: I am a student.
usage_note: 저 is the humble/formal first-person pronoun; also can mean ‘that’ as a demonstrative depending on context.

example_english: I'm watching a movie with a friend today.
usage_note: Informal first-person pronoun; avoid in formal situations—use 저 for politeness.

example_english: That person can't come today.
usage_note: '그' can mean 'that' or refer to a previously mentioned person; context determines gender (he/she).

example_korean: 우리 가족은 매주 일요일에 함께 식사해요.
example_english: Our family eats together every Sunday.
usage_note: '우리' can mean 'we' or 'our'; context determines whether it's subject or possessive.

example_korean: 회의에서 상대방의 의견을 먼저 들어 보세요.
example_english: In the meeting, please listen to the other party's opinion first.
usage_note: '상대방' refers to the other person/party in interactions; can be formal or neutral in contexts like meetings or negotiations.

example_english: Shall I bring you my book?
usage_note: 저의 is a formal/polite possessive; 저의 = 제 (less formal).

example_english: This is my book.
usage_note: Informal possessive used before nouns; polite sentence uses 내 with polite copula (이에요/예요).

example_english: You need to rest today.
usage_note: Used as polite 'you' but avoid with strangers; often used between spouses or in writing.

example_english: I will attend the meeting tomorrow.
usage_note: 내가 is the subject form of 'I' used for emphasis; polite verb ending used (해요체).

example_english: What you are saying now is correct.
usage_note: 네가 is informal 'you' used in casual contexts; avoid with strangers or superiors.

example_english: Are all of you gathered?
usage_note: Casual plural 'you'; avoid with elders—use 여러분 for politeness.
